The preceding section concludes the exposition on the essential tenets of the *Shejing* (Saṃyuktāgama). From here below begins the exposition of the *Zayi jing* (Saṃyuktapiṭaka). The text is divided as follows:
Second.
First, eleven.
Furthermore, there is a separate citation of a sutra for explanation.
Subsequently, the holy teaching is sustained by four dharmas.
The first sutra clarifies physical and mental seclusion, which induces realization as it truly is.
The second sutra concerns the thorough cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, through which one realizes what is to be known.
In the third [section], concerning skill in the mutual relationship between meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
the text is divided into three parts.
First, the scripture is cited as a heading.
The second part consists of two successive explanations of the four phrases of the sūtra.
The third part, beginning with "What is abiding? (*kathaṃ sthitiḥ*), provides a detailed explanation of the fourteen phrases of the sūtra.
By reversing the phrase "equal affection" (*samasneha*) to "unequal affection" (*viṣamasneha*), it constitutes one phrase, thereby completing the fourteen phrases.
Under the section on "The Phrase of Skillful Adjustment," there are two interpretations:
one that emphasizes the practice of skillful adjustment and another that emphasizes the adherence to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
These two headings are not explanations of the actual words of the sūtra.
Regarding the first of these four statements, a set of four propositions is established by correlating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with its objects.
There are eleven designations for *samāpatti* (equipoise);
first, the three primary *samādhis* are presented.
Regarding the four dharmas of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), one should apply the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Next, with the words "in this way" and so forth, the remaining ten qualities within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are illustrated;
likewise, the remaining two [qualities] among the six of meditative attainment are illustrated.
Each of these is further analyzed in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) by way of mutual correspondence.
This refers to the various samādhis, such as those characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*),
because they are most preeminent and because their objects of focus are transformative.
They each obtain their respective names.
Among the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) can produce transformations;
the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*).
Because it is mindless and tranquil,
it is singled out for mention.
Within the first of the two exclusive statements, "extinction" is raised at the outset to indicate the absence of perception (*asaṃjñika*).
Subsequently, the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality bases) are cited by way of analogy with the *abhibhvāyatana* (mastery bases);
since this is an abbreviated indication, their meaning can be understood.
In the second set of four statements, only the first two statements are formulated.

One who is skilled in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) but not skilled in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is one who thoroughly knows the distinctions among the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) pertaining to meditative concentration,
but is not [skilled] in entering meditative attainment.
Regarding the phrase "the distinctions among the characteristics and marks of all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*),
this refers to the nature of skillfulness in the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

It concerns whether one possesses skill or lacks skill regarding the distinctions of names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*) that serve as the designators for those meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Regarding meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), one can distinguish them based on whether there is skill or lack of skill in entering and emerging from them.
This can be understood through comparative analysis.

The first four lines clarify this by distinguishing between skill and unskillfulness in the functional operation of entering and emerging from the specific entities of concentration (*samādhi*) and attainment (*samāpatti*).
These two sets of four lines are composed by taking those meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) as being identical in essence but differing in meaning.
The Tripitaka Master said:
"This interpretation exists in the West."
The terms "samādhi" and so forth are explained as "samāpatti" (equipoise);
the essential nature of samādhi is termed "samāpatti.
Therefore, two phrases are employed.
Regarding the phrase "until one has heard from the Buddhas," this refers to three meanings concerning lack of skill in meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
first, not having heard it from the Buddha.
Second, they have not yet heard [the teachings] from a foremost bodhisattva;
third, they have not yet personally realized the ultimate goal themselves;
therefore, they lack skill regarding the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*).
The character "wei" (未) at the top penetrates down through three locations.
Jing said:
"Alternatively, the first stage may be designated as the 'first ultimate'."
Alternatively, the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) is designated as the "first ultimate.
That which is subsumed under the conceptualization of essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) pertains to scattered objects (*vikṣipta-viṣaya*),
because these are factors of a different category from those of the concentrated states (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
To contemplate scattered objects is called "emerging from meditative absorption.
Regarding "that which is to be done while in absorption," such as eating and so forth,
these are the tasks that ought to be performed upon emerging from absorption.
Because one must emerge from meditative absorption at this point,
the "characteristic of the object" refers to the essence of conceptualization;
by taking this as an object, one is able to enter various absorptions.
Because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are termed "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*),
that which is the object of meditative concentration is termed the "substance of conceptualization.
This is because, apart from its characteristics (*nimitta*), it is seen as having no separate nature.
Alternatively, this object of focus takes as its objective aspect the manifested characteristic (*nimitta*) of the body as it appears through discrimination among the five factors.
This is because, due to the meditative concentration already attained, one is unable to know anything beyond this, and so forth.
This explains that those in the three lower stages do not know those above.
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, it says:
"One who, relying on the four dhyānas, knows the minds of those in the formless realm."
Because this is explained with reference to great bodhisattvas, there is no contradiction.
"Inducing" refers to the ability to briefly summarize the extensive meaning of words and phrases;
this power of hearing and retention encompasses that extensive meaning.

Regarding the phrase "What is meant by 'equal affection'? It refers to affection characterized by shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)," this means that twelve factors necessarily arise prior [to concentration]. These are:
first, shame; second, dread of blame; and so on, up to the twelfth, joy (*prīti*).
By means of this skillful method, the mind attains concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding this, the Tripiṭaka Master says:
"Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the mental state that serves as the skillful method for concentration."
Because it loves the supreme qualities of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it is called "loving attainment" (*samāpattiruci*).
Jing says:
"Shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*), among others, are all in accordance with the True Dharma."
"Equanimity of affection" (samacchanda) refers to right principle and right affection.
Ji states:
"Because one possesses equal affection toward these twelve [objects], it is called 'equanimity of affection.'"
There are two types of skillful means:
first, the path of increasing and decreasing;
second, the [three] of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity.
As previously explained among the thirty-two marks,
there are four sections in the fourth sūtra, the *Vibhaṅga-dhyāna-sūtra*: first,
the citation of the sūtra as a heading.
Second, a brief explanation of the four turnings;
third, a detailed explanation of their characteristics;
fourth, the conclusion.
Regarding the statement "the four turnings should be known" and "the two times are inverted," this is the explanation of Master Ki (Kaiyuan).
Regarding the four types of reversal: first, the reversal occurring when proceeding toward a contaminated (*sāsrava*) samādhi;
second, the reversal occurring when retreating from a contaminated concentration;
and third, the non-reversal occurring when one is currently losing a contaminated concentration.
There is no error when advancing toward the four untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
Alternatively, regarding the first two [stages], to claim that advancing constitutes retreating is called "inversion.
This refers to the case where one claims to be retreating while actually advancing toward the tainted concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*).
Furthermore, when one proceeds from an untainted meditative absorption, it is called "receding.
Therefore, all such states are termed "inversions.
Thus says the Treatise.
Regarding the second point, the inversion at the time of falling away from samādhi:
when one practices for the advancement of the untainted (anāsrava) but falls back into the tainted (sāsrava), this is called inversion.
Regarding the latter two types of falling away, falling away itself is termed non-inversion.
Initially, when one actually regresses from an impure (*sāsrava*) meditative absorption, it is called "regression.
Subsequently, when one regresses from a pure (*anāsrava*) absorption to an impure one, it is called "regressing from the impure absorption.
Within the section on regression, there are three successive expositions.
First, one falls away due to relishing the flavor [of meditative attainment];
second, one falls away due to arrogance and contempt;
third, one falls away due to greed and deception.
The second non-erroneous [cognition] should be understood as the reverse of the first non-erroneous [cognition].
Its characteristic is this: when one is about to lose an impure concentration and has attained a pure concentration, one knows the regression as it truly is.
This is called non-erroneousness.
Third, non-erroneousness is knowing one's retreat when falling back from untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
Fourth, non-erroneousness is knowing that there is retreat from the tainted (*sāsrava*) when advancing toward the untainted.
Regarding the difference between this fourth [case] and the previous second:
in the former, one practices the means for the untainted (anāsrava) but has not yet realized it, which is called "retrogression from a previously attained concentration.
In the present fourth case, one actually attains the untainted so that the tainted (sāsrava) no longer functions; this is what is termed "retrogression."
Thus, the distinction is established. Jing says:
"The second 'non-erroneous' (aviparyāsa) is the inverse of the first 'non-erroneous'."
How should its characteristics be understood?
First is the preparatory concentration of retrogression;
second is the fundamental concentration of retrogression.

Therefore, it is said that this reverses what preceded. These latter two types of regression both refer to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who, having suppressed the afflictions, fall back from their state. Regarding the phrase "by relying on such [a basis], one establishes the four transitions": *The term "regression" (parihāṇi) refers to falling back from a previously attained state due to the arising of afflictions. There are three kinds of regression: first, regression from what has been attained; second, regression from what was not yet attained; and third, regression from the fruit itself. Among these, regression from what has been attained is of two types: regression from the path and regression from the fruit. Regression from the path is also of two types: regression from the mundane path and regression from the supramundane path. Regression from the mundane path is further divided into two: regression from the path of preparation and regression from the path of liberation. Regression from the supramundane path is likewise of two types: regression from the path of seeing and regression from the path of cultivation. Regression from the fruit is also of two types: regression from the fruit of stream-entry and regression from the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship. Regression from what was not yet attained refers to failing to attain a higher stage when one should have done so.

Regression from the fruit itself refers to falling away from the state of being established in any of the four fruits.* By relying on such distinctions, the four transitions are established. Specifically, these four transitions are: 1) the transition of falling back; 2) the transition of remaining as is; 3) the transition of advancing; and 4) the transition of transcending. These are established based on the aforementioned classifications of regression and non-regression. Thus, the four transitions are formulated in accordance with the various modes of progress and decline among practitioners.
This means that because one relies on these two non-erroneous [perspectives] regarding arising and decline, the four turnings are established;
thus it is concluded.
Fifth is the analysis of the four examinations of conduct.
The text contains three sections:
first, the citation of the sūtra as a heading;
second, a brief exposition on examining the characteristics of practice.
Third, the detailed exposition:
that which is examined consists of the fourfold purity and meditative concentration (*śamatha*),
while that which performs the examination consists of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, a single person may practice all four types;
the four categories, beginning with the inferior portion,
are respectively correlated with the four states, beginning with the stage of regression.
The explanation follows the text.
Regarding the sixth [point], it concerns not apprehending perception or non-perception with respect to the six objects.
As for the statement in the Sūtra that one does not at all experience these various phenomena, whether they be real or existent:
One does not grasp at the specific characteristics of objects.
If one does not even grasp at perceptions—meaning one does not grasp at the perceptions of the six sense-objects—how much less would one grasp at that which is non-perceptual?
One does not grasp at that non-perception either.
The subsequent passage states: "The explanation that there is no mark of the eye does not even admit of perception (*saṃjñā*);
the explanation that it does not admit of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not admit of anything at all;
since it does not admit of non-perception (*asaṃjñā*), how much less could it admit of the absence of perception (*niḥsaṃjñā*)?"
Regarding the statement, "Because of the destruction through revulsion, one’s power is eclipsed," and so forth, up to "there remains the perception of them":
this means that through repeated revulsion by means of the untainted (anāsrava) [path], one subsequently forms the perception of non-existence regarding the eye and other [sense bases].
Only the conceptualization of the various principles of the Four Noble Truths arises;
one who does not accept ideation or non-ideation does not accept either ideation or non-ideation at all.
Because one does not engage in mental reflection upon any perceptions, both the perception of emptiness and the perception of existence are entirely not accepted;
thus, within the principle of the suchness of cessation, one contemplates tranquility.
The meaning intended here is that being "without conceptualization" (*asaṃjñin*) refers to the state where all characteristics of conceptualization are abandoned.
When non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) directly realizes suchness (*tathatā*),
it is likewise free from the prior characteristics of suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
Thus, one is detached from both perception and non-perception;
therefore, being detached from the perception of signs is called "non-perception.
Furthermore, it is said that one abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth.
This is based on the fact that [the cessation of perception] arises from the various perceptions of that state of meditative absorption;
it explains the preceding scriptural passage that one does not even admit perception, let alone non-perception.
Seventh, regarding the explanation of the Sūtra on the Paths of the Four Destinies:
When first becoming an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one attains the fundamental dhyānas;
later, upon hearing the Dharma, one is able to induce the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This is also called "cultivating those untainted (*anāsrava*) superior perceptions based on the superior mind (*adhicitta*)."
That second person, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, attains the first fruit (*srotāpatti*).
Desiring to suddenly sever the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across the nine stages in order to realize arhatship,
they suppress the afflictions of cultivation belonging to the desire realm from the moment of attaining the first fruit.
The attainment of the fundamental dhyānas with outflows and so forth is called the cultivation of the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
because the regression from those with outflows is designated as the path of meditation.
It is also called the cultivation of the higher mind (*adhicitta*) based on the superior perception (*adhisaṃjñā*).
Regarding the third type of practitioner, who is said to "attain both śamatha and vipaśyanā together through their simultaneous and alternating operation":
such a person, while still an ordinary being, first suppresses the afflictions of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
One is able to first give rise to the fundamental dhyāna;
subsequently, relying on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration, one enters the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and attains the third fruit.
Attaining entry into the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) is called "progressing toward and inducing the higher mind and wisdom."
It also leads to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Therefore, the conclusion below states:
"The twenty-third [point] is because it leads to the path of cultivation."
The fourth type of practitioner first attains contaminated meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Subsequently, by hearing the Dharma, they enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and realize the third fruit; this is called "inducing the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*).
In this manner, they gradually eliminate the remaining afflictions of the path of cultivation.
It also leads toward the path by inducing the path of an Arhat, thereby inducing the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The conclusion below states: "The fourth [stage] is the path leading toward [the goal], because it induces both.
According to this principle, such a person likewise relies upon the higher mind (*adhicitta*) to induce higher wisdom (*adhijñāna*).
However, it differs from the first person who cites only the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*);
because it cites all three paths, it is established separately as the fourth.
Regarding the eighth [topic], there are three parts within the explanation of the *Catuḥśukla-viśeṣasūtra*.
First, the title of the *Vimalaviśeṣa-sūtra* is presented;
second, the meaning of its purity and excellence is explained;
third, the characteristics of its purity and excellence are explained.
Regarding the phrase "the precepts and so forth that are obtained, realized, and induced":
"obtained" refers to those dharmas that are perfected;
"realized" refers to those dharmas that are embraced.
Regarding "the precepts and so forth that are induced," this refers to exerting diligent effort to bring what is incomplete to completion.
As for the four purities and excellences,
the first is ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Second, the samādhis;
third, the views;
fourth, the liberations.
In this context, the terms "precepts" and so forth, which are cited as being "not to be abandoned" and "to be realized," all pertain to the excellence of the four purities (*catasraḥ pariśuddhayaḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "perfectly embracing," it is explained as follows:
to exert diligent effort so that what is incomplete becomes complete constitutes the precepts, concentration, and view that are cited here.
Because it is the essence of liberation (*vimukti*), it is not explicitly cited and explained.
Furthermore, that which is "attained" is morality (*śīla*); that which is "realized" is concentration (*samādhi*) and vision (*darśana*);
and that which is "induced" is liberation (*vimukti*).
The phrase "precepts and so forth" includes concentration, view, essence, and liberation.
Furthermore, that which is attained is the precepts,
and that which is realized is concentration.
That which is induced consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and liberation (*vimukti*);
for brevity, the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) is omitted.
Furthermore, both wisdom and knowledge-vision may be termed "right view" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), which fully encompasses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
What are the seven lower [factors]?
The first is ethical discipline (*śīla*).
How are the two each for concentration (*samādhi*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), and liberation (*vimukti*)?
These should be explained accordingly.
Although he abides in the four categories and six branches, such as the possession of complete ethical discipline (*śīla*),
they are explained in detail in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
The two types, ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), are termed "perfected" during the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
Upon entering the stage of a noble one (*ārya*), they are further embraced.
Within meditative concentration, there are two kinds.
First, at the time of detachment from desire, the first six mental orientations have not yet attained the fundamental [dhyāna] and thus are not called "perfected.
If one attains the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage, one attains the fundamental dhyāna and is called "perfected."
The attainment of the first three lower dhyānas is not yet termed "complete";
only upon attaining the fourth is it called complete.
This liberation belongs to the stage of training (śaikṣa).
That which is not yet perfected in the stage of no-more-learning is called "perfected";
that which is liberation not [dependent on] specific times is called "embraced liberation";
and the analytical cessation obtained through the removal of hindrances to meditative concentration and hindrances to objective matters is called "liberation."
Regarding the ninth [section], the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇabhikṣu-pañcalakṣaṇasūtra-vyākhyā*:
"Various evil and unwholesome thoughts such as desire" refers to unwholesome thoughts of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*),

ill will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), and harm (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*), as well as thoughts concerning relatives (*jñāti-vitarka*), the country (*janapada-vitarka*), immortality (*amara-vitarka*), and the enjoyment of past pleasures (*pūrva-krīḍita-vitarka*).
The seven types of vitarka and vicāra all constitute the essence of the hindrances.
The phrase "briefly, there are three types of persons" and so forth is a general heading that indicates three categories of discursive thought.
The distinctions constitute five types;
they are explained individually below.
First is the practitioner of investigation who is of the weak grade.
By contemplating the characteristics of the truths, such as cause and effect, one causes the seven types of discursive thought (*vitarka*) to cease.
Based on intermediate-level discursive thought, two kinds are distinguished:
first, contemplating the faults and afflictions (*ādīnava*) of discursive thought.
Second, by means of non-recollection and non-attention, one causes the seven types of discursive thought (*vitarka*) to cease.
Based on superior discursive thought, this is further divided into two:
first, not causing them all to cease immediately from the outset.
One must employ skillful means to gradually subdue it.
Second, if one is still unable to subdue it and consequently gives rise to weariness or fear,
one should contemplate extensively so as to cause the seven types of vitarka to cease.
The tenth section, the *Dhūtaguṇa-sūtra-vyākhyāna*, consists of three parts:
first, citing the sūtra and posing the question;
second, explaining [the meaning]; and third, the analogy of the three refinements.
The three methods of formal accusation are combined as follows:
just as the raw gold existing within the nature of gold is placed below,
so too is the initial generation of the mind and renunciation of the world called the "first smelting and refining."
On the stage of the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*), one attains the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth;
this serves as a refinement for entering the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*).
Because it is a subsequent refinement, the treatise states that one is no longer constrained by conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
By relying on the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), one subdues [the afflictions] so that the lineage of the faculties becomes manifest;
because the faculties eliminate the afflictions, they are designated by the term "refined" (*paribhāvita*).
Regarding the third of the three characteristics mentioned in the eleventh commentary on the *Saṃjñāparyāyavarga Sūtra*:
The three are: (1) calming, (2) exertion, and (3) equanimity.

Calming and exertion are exclusively cultivated during the preparatory stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) when there is incorrect investigation regarding dependent origination and so forth.
Because he does not engage in analytical reflection, his mind is not in right concentration;
thus he cannot realize the truths and exhaust all outflows.
By repeatedly contemplating equanimity and then reflecting upon dependent origination, he eventually fulfills the path to the exhaustion of outflows and becomes an Arhat.
The preceding eleven sections provide separate scriptural citations for explanation.
First, furthermore, regarding the threefold way in which the holy teaching is sustained by the four correct dharmas: first, the heading;
second, the detailed classification; third, the explanation.
"Seclusion" refers to the place where one enters meditative concentration.
"That which is practiced" refers to the cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom.
"The fruit of cultivation" refers to the liberation attained, as well as the unconditioned fruits resulting from the abandonment of the two obstacles.
"How is it that one who has already practiced *śamatha*?"—this explains the third [point].
All those who possess grasping are those who grasp at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
They grasp at all that exists.
The cessation of this attachment to phenomena is called the "element of cessation" (nirodhadhātu).
The three elements mentioned here differ from those explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* below.
They also state that the complete abandonment of the delusions of views is called the "element of abandonment" (prahāṇadhātu);
the complete abandonment of the delusions of cultivation is called the "element of detachment" (vairāgyadhātu);
and the complete abandonment of all remaining contaminated phenomena (sāsravadharma) is called the "element of cessation" (nirodhadhātu).
The *Kṣudraka-śāstra* states that the abandonment of the eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) is called the element of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*).
The abandonment of the fetter of craving (*upādānasaṃyojana*) is called the element of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*).
The cessation of all other contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) is called the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
Regarding "those who are without discord":
the general meaning intends to clarify that because the Buddha and his disciples perceive the same reality, the meanings they teach are identical;
their words and phrases do not differ, and as they accord with one another, there is no discord.
The Buddha-dharma abides for a long time, bringing benefit and happiness to a vast extent, its fame and so forth providing thorough nourishment.
It is not like the non-Buddhist paths, which give rise to divergent views and tenets with variations in phrasing;
herein, whether in meaning, phrase, or expression, nothing is left unsaid.
Because the beginning and the end are cited to encompass the middle:
as for the first phrase,
it refers to the preceding phrase, and one asks by means of this very phrase.
Regarding the second [category],
this briefly clarifies the equal moistening and harmonization within the phrases.
It is largely consistent with what was transmitted by Jingtai Beiji.
For example, when the Venerable Ānanda was among five hundred bhikṣus, he questioned one bhikṣu with this opening phrase,
and then questioned a second bhikṣu, and so on, up to the fifth hundred.
They all replied, "So it is, so it is.
This is what is called the meaning of the relationship between teacher and disciple: there is no discordance, but rather a state of equal and harmonious moisture, with mutual accord.
The subsequent passage serves as a counter-illustration, stating that even if one were to ask based on the first [of the five] aggregates, and so forth.
Suppose that one person asks about the impermanence of the aggregates (*skandha*) based on the first [topic],
while another person subsequently asks about the impermanence of the elements (*dhātu*) based on the second;
then this cannot be called an equal and harmonious inquiry regarding the first point.
Now, according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*,
it cites a sūtra stating that Ānanda went to ask the Elder named Vimukta about the meaning of liberation,
and the Elder named Vimukta replied that one should cultivate two dharmas.
Thus, one attains the fruit of liberation from the three realms.
Ānanda next asked about the names of the five hundred senior disciples (*sthavira*), each of whom answered individually,
without contradicting the senior disciple.
Go and ask the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata will answer as the Elder named Śreṇika understands:
because one has severed all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), it is called the "element of severance" (*prahāṇadhātu*).
Because it is free from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), it is called the "element of detachment" (*vairāgyadhātu*);
because it extinguishes all conditioned formations, it is called the "element of cessation" (*nirodhadhātu*).
This is explained in detail in that treatise.
This is called the Elder and his disciples seeing things as identical to the Tathāgata’s response to Ānanda’s question;
it is equally moistening and harmonious in its doctrine and meaning, conforming to them without a hair’s breadth of deviation.
Therefore, it is called "without conflict" (*araṇa*). 7.

Non-Samāhita-bhūmi (Part 5, Upper). Among the four stages of the objective sphere of the non-Samāhita-bhūmi, this is the second section below, which explains the stage that is not in meditative equipoise (*asamāhita*).
The *Śāstra* commentary states that by reversing the preceding [definition], it becomes easy to understand.

Within the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is taught that in *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the ālayavijñāna is eternally extinguished.
If this is so, does the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) increase or decrease?
The commentary states:
Throughout the various sūtras and śāstras, it is said that the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases,
because sentient beings have existed from time immemorial and are not newly produced.
There is no increase, yet there is the immeasurable.
When those of the two vehicles with fixed natures enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, they fall into the category of non-birth;
thus, in principle, there is also decrease.
Because they are predominant, it is said that there is no decrease,
just like a single drop of water in the ocean.
However, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts, Śreṇika asks whether the body exists prior to the afflictions.
If afflictions come first,
and if the body comes first,
how can it be said that it is only because of afflictions that the body exists?
"If afflictions precede [the body], by whom were they created, and where do they abide?
The Buddha answered Śreṇika:
"Although afflictions and the body arise simultaneously and lack any sequence of before or after,"
The reason one acquires a body due to afflictions, and afflictions do not arise because of the body,

the Buddha responds by appealing to their own premise of beginninglessness.
Thus, one knows that there is no increase.
Furthermore, according to the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*,
the realm of sentient beings is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because all sentient beings share this unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta*),

The intended meaning of that sutra is that the realm of sentient beings is established based on the arising of delusion from reality.

Although those of the two vehicles enter the remainderless state where all aggregates are extinguished,

Regarding "mindfulness (smṛti) pertaining to both categories":

This reveals that its intrinsic nature consists of the maturation-born sensation of the hindrance to meditative concentration, along with the ignorance concomitant therewith;

Second, the desire to seize and plunder, which arises from a lack of restraint;

nor does one wish to take them as one's own wives, concubines, servants, or slaves.
Regarding the phrase "named 'Non-appropriation of All Desires,' raining down various views, etc.":
according to the custom of the Western Regions, a year consists of three seasons, known as the *trikāla*.
From the sixteenth day of the first month until the fifteenth day of the fifth month is called the "hot season" (*uṣṇakāla*).
Because it is extremely hot at this time,

Because the *Sāṃkhya* school holds that the primary cause arises during the "Rainy Season" (*varṣā*), it is so named.
The followers of Vṛṣagaṇa are called the Vṛṣagaṇas.

The *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* are the excellent conditions that serve as the causes for the arising of this discourse.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* is the favorable condition for the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*);

one should not engage in debate out of attachment to evil matters or by giving rise to malicious speech;

Regarding the statement, "The meaning to be established has two [aspects]:

its intrinsic nature and its specific difference," herein, the thesis and so forth are termed the "means of establishment" (sādhana), while the intrinsic nature and specific difference are termed the "object to be established" (sādhya).
Prior to Vasubandhu, the school was called the "Prover" (sādhana);
from Dignāga onwards, the school was called the "Proven" (sādhya).
Master Fami said:
In reality, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is also that which is to be established (*sādhya*).
Within the process of establishment, if the subject and object were not distinguished, there would be no basis for the mind’s engagement.
Therefore, following Dignāga, the thesis is termed "that which is to be established."
Master Ji’s commentary explains that this has three layers. First,
it is said that the meaning established by the thesis statement is called the "probandum" (the object to be established).
Therefore, regarding what is established here, there is a meaningful statement:
the words that express the thesis (*pakṣa*), as well as the words expressing the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, are all termed the "means of proof" (*sādhana*).

Although the words expressing the thesis are also "that which is to be proven" (*sādhya*) because they are established by means of the reason and the example, [they are classified here among the means of proof].

The following passage explains that because it first demonstrates the tenet one personally accepts and delights in, and because it is what is established rather than that which is not yet established,
it is called a "proof" (*sādhana*) simply because it functions as a proof for the meaning to be established, just as a reason (*hetu*) or an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) functions as a proof.
The determined meaning expressed is exclusively that which is established;
it alone is called "that which is to be proven.
Second, [others] say that the intrinsic nature and specific differences of the collection of all phenomena, whether according to scripture or reasoning, are both that which is established.
Since both the name and the meaning exist accordingly in this context,
that which is set forth by one party against an opponent—

whether it be a statement or a meaning, whether in its essential nature (*svabhāva*) or its specific qualification (*viśeṣa*)— is called a "proposition" (*pakṣa*); when it functions as such, it is termed a "proof" (*sādhana*).

Although other schools [of thought] are also included within the category of the "probandum" (*sādhya*) and the "probans" (*sādhana*), they receive the name "probans" because they constitute the general class of such [means].

The excellence of the momentary destruction of the present realm (*kṣaṇa*) is established as its locus and root-basis (*mūla-pratiṣṭhāpana*),
just as the root is the foundation of a tree.
Therefore, the root of sound is called the "root-source" (*mūla*);
this refers to the syllable itself.
The location from which the sound emerges is called the "location" (*sthāna*).
Because it emerged from the source of sound, it is the original Śabdavidyā (Science of Phonetics).
This refers to its origin at the beginning of the kalpa,
when Brahmā created one million verses of Śabdavidyā.
Later, it was abridged by Maitreya;
Śakra further condensed it into one hundred thousand verses.
Subsequently, the seer Kātyāyanīputra condensed it into twelve thousand verses.
Next, there was the sage Pāṇini, who composed a summary in eight thousand verses.
These four treatises mentioned above are collectively termed the "Locales" (Pradeśa).
Of these, only the latter two are currently extant.
The two preceding treatises have both already vanished.
As for the foundational grammar (*śabdavidyā*) concerning the root forms of characters, there are three hundred verses;
these are the abridged grammatical verses composed by the Sage Pāṇini.
Thereafter, there was the *Hetuvāda* (Discourse on Causes), consisting of eight sections and comprising eight hundred stanzas;
it is titled *Pratyaya*.
Furthermore, there was the *Śākyasūtra-vyākhyāna* (Exegesis of the Śākya Discourse), consisting of one thousand five hundred stanzas.
Furthermore, there is the *Unnādi-śāstra* in two thousand five hundred stanzas.
These five systems of grammatical science (*śabda-vidyā*) are collectively termed "Roots" (*mūla*),
because they serve as the fundamental basis for generating knowledge and understanding within the foundational field of grammar (*mūla-sthāna-śabda-vidyā*).
However, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla composed the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra-vicitra-ratna* in twenty-five thousand stanzas;
this work is regarded in the West as the ultimate treatise on grammar and is widely prevalent in the world.
